caption: {name}: waste per person and the economy, compared with 2011
general_note: Both lines start at 100 in 2011, so you can compare how fast each one grew: 110 means 10% more than in 2011. The economy is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation (2020 prices). When the blue line is above the orange one, the economy grew faster than waste. This is called decoupling.
break_note: Some countries changed what they count: Luxembourg (from 2016), Czechia (from 2017) and Belgium, Austria and Slovakia (from 2020) started counting waste from businesses, so their waste per person jumped by 14% to 75% in one year without more waste being generated. The EU figure includes these jumps. Pick one of these countries to see the year of its change.

country_notes.note: The EU figure includes the countries that changed what they count, so the real rise in waste is probably smaller than the line shows.

From 2017 Czechia also counts similar waste from businesses. Its waste per person jumped by 44% in one year: a change in counting, not more waste generated. Before the change, waste grew more slowly than the economy.

From 2020 Belgium also counts similar waste from businesses. Its waste per person jumped by 75% in one year: a change in counting, not more waste generated. Before the change, waste per person fell while the economy grew.

From 2020 Austria also counts waste from shops and businesses. Its waste per person jumped by 42% in one year: a change in counting, not more waste generated. Before the change, waste grew more slowly than the economy.

From 2020 Slovakia also counts waste from businesses, which raised its waste per person by 14% in one year. But its waste was already growing faster than its economy before that: +35% against +22% from 2011 to 2019.

From 2016 Luxembourg counts more waste from sources other than homes. Its waste per person jumped by 34% in one year: a change in counting, not more waste generated. Before the change, waste per person fell while the economy stayed about the same.
From 2014 Estonia also counts packaging waste. Its waste per person rose by 22% in one year, when it started counting packaging waste. Before the change, waste per person fell while the economy grew.
From 2013 Slovenia also counts waste from special waste collectors. Its waste per person rose by 14% in one year, partly because of this change.

Ireland's GDP per person jumped by 23.5% in 2015 alone, mostly because multinational companies moved assets such as intellectual property to Ireland (Irish Central Statistics Office). So the economy looks bigger than it is, and decoupling looks stronger than it is; the fall in waste per person is not affected. Ireland also changed how it estimates household waste in 2014, and there are no waste figures for 2013 and 2015.
